reader.summary: During this window, the dominant story was the continued legal proceedings against former President Nicolás Maduro in New York, where he and his wife pleaded not guilty to US charges of conspiracy to torture. The judge cut Maduro off as he attempted to deliver a personal statement, and he publicly called the new allegations false. Simultaneously, Washington signaled a thaw in bilateral relations by lifting sanctions on Jorge Rodríguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, a move described by multiple outlets as a new gesture of rapprochement. On the economic front, Venezuela's acting president announced expectations of nearly $76 billion in oil investment over the next five years, while the World Bank indicated it could extend up to $5 billion in loans to the country. The top economic adviser stressed that debt restructuring was a priority and that a debt sustainability analysis would be published very soon. Centerview was confirmed as Venezuela's ongoing financial adviser. In a related political development, opposition figure María Corina Machado topped the latest polls as US-backed negotiations resumed. The US Space Force also displayed weapons it said were used in operations involving Venezuela. In regional news, Chile sentenced a Venezuelan gang member to 20 years for the kidnapping and killing of a dissident.

display.eli5:
Here's what's happening in Venezuela right now. Former president Nicolás Maduro is sitting in a New York courtroom, and he just told the judge the torture charges against him are wrong. The trial is far from over—next week the judge will set the schedule for what happens next, like what documents each side has to share with each other. That's the Maduro torture trial, the big lead story.

Meanwhile, Venezuela's government has been making a lot of promises about money. They said they expect tens of billions of dollars in oil investment, and the World Bank hinted at a big loan. Next week, they're supposed to actually publish a detailed plan showing how they'll handle their massive debt. That document—the debt sustainability analysis—is the key piece that banks and lenders need before they really write the check.

The US is also slowly easing up on Venezuela. They already lifted sanctions on one top politician, and next week more banks or officials could get the same treatment. This is all tied to talks that María Corina Machado is leading on the opposition side, where everyone's trying to figure out when the next presidential election happens.

A real surprise would be if Maduro's lawyers suddenly asked the judge to let him out on bail. That would be dramatic because he's a former president and the charges are serious, but it's not impossible. Nobody expects a verdict next week, though.
